questions.question: For $x\ge0$ and a positive integer $n$, how is the nonnegative real root $x^{1/n}$ defined using a supremum?
options: As $\sup\{y\in\mathbb{R}\colon y\ge0,\ y^n\ge x\}$
As $\inf\{y\in\mathbb{R}\colon y\ge0,\ y^n\le x\}$
As $\sup\{y\in\mathbb{R}\colon y\ge0,\ y^n\le x\}$
As $\sup\{y\in\mathbb{R}\colon y\ge0,\ ny\le x\}$

questions.question: For $x\ge0$, what is $\left(x^{1/n}\right)^n$?
options: $x^n$

questions.question: Why does the definition use $y^n\le x$ rather than $y^n=x$ in $\{y\ge0\colon\,\cdot\,\}$?
options: It yields a nonempty set bounded above, so the supremum exists
Because the equation $y^n=x$ can have several distinct solutions
Because using $\le$ makes the resulting root come out larger
Because the equality $y^n=x$ is in fact never attained

questions.question: For $x=16$, compare $16^{1/2}$ and $16^{1/4}$.
options: both equal $8$

questions.question: Does the supremum in $x^{1/n}=\sup\{y\ge0\colon y^n\le x\}$ belong to the set?
options: Yes: $x^{1/n}$ satisfies $(x^{1/n})^n\le x$, so it lies in the set
No: like $1=\sup\,(0,1)$, a supremum always lies outside its set
Only when $x^{1/n}$ is rational; otherwise it is a limit outside the set
Only when $x\ge1$, because for $0<x<1$ the root $x^{1/n}$ exceeds $x$

questions.question: Using the course convention for odd roots, what is $(-8)^{1/3}$?
options: It is not a real number.

questions.question: Which monotonicity property does the principal $n$-th root function have on $[0,+\infty)$, for a positive integer $n$?
options: It is decreasing on $[0,+\infty)$.
It is increasing only when $n$ is even.
It is decreasing on $[0,1]$ and increasing on $[1,+\infty)$.
It is increasing on $[0,+\infty)$.

questions.question: Using the supremum definition, what is $0^{1/n}$ for a positive integer $n$?
options: It is undefined, because the definition needs $x>0$.

questions.question: Which statement gives the real-domain rule for $n$-th roots when $n$ is a positive integer?
options: Every positive integer index allows every real input $x$.
Every positive integer index requires a nonnegative input $x$.
Even indices allow all real inputs; odd indices require $x\ge0$.
Even indices require $x\ge0$; odd indices allow every real $x$.

questions.question: For $x=4$ and $n=2$, which number belongs to the defining set $\{y\in\mathbb{R}\colon y\ge0,\ y^2\le4\}$?
For a positive integer $n$ and $x\ge0$, which fact about $y\mapsto y^n$ on $[0,\infty)$ shows that $y^n=x$ has at most one solution $y\ge0$?
options: $0\le u<v$ implies $u^n<v^n$.
$0\le y\le1$ implies $0\le y^n\le1$.
Some $y\ge0$ has $y^n>x$.
$(-y)^n=y^n$ when $n$ is even.

questions.question: For $0<x<1$ and an integer $n\ge2$, how does $x^{1/n}$ compare with $x$?
options: It depends on whether $n$ is even

questions.question: Which fact guarantees that $\sup\{y\ge0\colon y^n\le x\}$ exists for every $x\ge0$?
options: The set is nonempty and bounded above, and $\mathbb{R}$ is complete
Every nonempty set of real numbers attains a maximum element
The set in question contains only finitely many points
The argument $x$ is required to be a rational number
